item.title: Stormwater Fee on Your Water Bill: What You
item.description:
Quick Answer

A stormwater fee covers the cost of managing rainwater runoff from streets and properties. It is usually a flat monthly charge on your water or utility bill, separate from your water usage charges. You typically cannot reduce it by using less water, but some utilities offer discounts for installing permeable surfaces or rain barrels.

What Is a Stormwater Fee Exactly?

To understand the stormwater fee on water bill, you must first understand the difference between a utility service and a tax. Many municipalities explicitly state that this charge is a user fee, not a tax. For example, the City of Alexandria, Virginia, clarifies on its official website that the Stormwater Utility Fee is included as a separate line item on the real estate tax bill but is "not a tax." It is a utility user fee modeled after how residents are billed for other services like water and sewer.

item.title: Sewer Averaging Explained: Why Your Sewer Charge Does Not Match Summer Use
item.description:
The problem: your sewer charge stays high even when your summer use drops

You cut back on outdoor watering, your water use goes down, but the sewer charge barely moves. That mismatch makes a lot of people think the bill is wrong.

In most cities, the sewer line is not metered directly. Instead, the utility estimates your wastewater based on a winter average or a fixed seasonal formula. Once you understand that system, the charge makes more sense.

item.title: How Sewer Charges Work on Your Water Bill (and Why They Can Be Higher Than Water)
item.description:
Quick Answer

Sewer charges pay for collecting and treating the water that leaves your home. Most residential sewer bills are based on your water usage (often measured in [CCF](/blog/what-is-ccf-on-a-water-bill/)), a "winter average" (also called [sewer averaging](/blog/sewer-averaging-water-bill-explained/)), or a flat monthly fee. Sewer can cost more than water because wastewater treatment is expensive and carries large fixed costs. You usually cannot remove the fixed fee, but you can often lower the usage-based part by fixing leaks — a [running toilet can waste 200+ gallons per day](/blog/is-your-toilet-running-leak-test/), so check this first and cutting indoor water use.

item.title: Is Your Toilet Running? A Simple Leak Test (and How It Shows Up on Your Water Bill)
item.description:
Quick Answer: The 10-Minute Toilet Leak Test

A running toilet can waste 200–400 gallons per day and add $50–$100+ to your water bill. Here is how to test for one right now:

  1. Remove the toilet tank lid.
  2. Add 5–10 drops of food coloring (or a dye tablet) to the tank water.
  3. Wait 10–15 minutes without flushing.
  4. Check the bowl. If any color appears in the bowl, your flapper is leaking.
  5. If color appears: The flapper valve needs replacing (a $10–$15 part, 15-minute DIY fix).

Want to confirm with your water meter? Turn off all water, check the leak indicator dial, and see if it moves. If it does and the toilet test is negative, you may have a hidden leak elsewhere.
